title: Atmospheric dynamics of terrestrial exoplanets over a wide range of orbital and atmospheric parameters
notes: Confirmed on IOP page (published 4 May 2015). arXiv:1407.6349. Idealized moist GCM varying rotation rate, stellar flux, atmospheric mass, gravity, optical thickness, radius.
quantitative: From arXiv:1407.6349 (ar5iv): rotation rates simulated 1/24 to 12 x Earth (Fig. 5 subset 1/16..8). 'more jets ... develop' as rotation increases; jet count tied to eddy length scale, which 'scales inversely with rotation rate' (no numeric jet counts in text; only in Figs. 4, 6). Hadley cell width compared against Held & Hou axisymmetric prediction proportional to Omega^-1 (Fig. 6a reference line); simulations follow the trend but eddies complicate it; at very slow rotation Hadley cells become nearly global. Faster rotation -> larger equator-to-pole dT, relatively flat below Omega_E and strong above; eddy vs mean transport cross over at ~0.2 Omega_E. Slow rotation: subtropical jets at high latitude; fast: Hadley cells/subtropical jets contract equatorward and eddy-driven jets appear at high latitude.

authors: Yang, J.; Cowan, N. B.; Abbot, D. S.
title: Stabilizing cloud feedback dramatically expands the habitable zone of tidally locked planets
notes: Confirmed on IOP page. Tidally locked planets remain habitable at about twice the stellar flux of earlier 1D estimates; substellar convective clouds raise albedo.
quantitative: From article body (as summarised by fetch): M-star case at 2200 W m^-2 -> albedo 0.53, max surface T ~305 K; at 1600 W m^-2 removing clouds drops albedo 0.53 -> 0.04 and raises global-mean Ts 246 K -> 319 K (73 K cloud cooling).

authors: Adriani, A.; Mura, A.; Orton, G.; et al. (32 authors)
title: Clusters of cyclones encircling Jupiter's poles
quantitative: North pole: 8 circumpolar cyclones around a single polar cyclone; South pole: 5 circumpolar cyclones around a polar cyclone (Juno JIRAM/JunoCam, first five orbits). South polar cyclone centre drifted 88.0S (PJ1) -> 89.0S (PJ4) -> 88.4S (PJ5) (extended data). No precedent on other planets.

authors: Barbosa Aguiar, A. C.; Read, P. L.; Wordsworth, R. D.; Salter, T.; Yamazaki, Y. H.
title: A laboratory model of Saturn's North Polar Hexagon
notes: DOI resolves to Elsevier pii S0019103509004382; title, authors, Icarus, 2010, pp. 755-763 confirmed on secondary catalogue pages (openpolar.no ORA record; isc.ac inventory). Volume 206 seen only in ADS bibcode 2010Icar..206..755B (search-result URL); Elsevier page could not be rendered. Author initials as in my request are consistent with the catalogue but the catalogue name fields were garbled.
quantitative: Abstract: hexagon at ~76N; wave modes from nonlinear equilibration of barotropically unstable zonal jets; linear instability analysis of Saturn's winds consistent with a north hexagon and no south counterpart. Per review arXiv:1609.09626 (Saturn's Polar Atmosphere) describing this paper: with unbounded deformation radius 'the maximum growth rate occurs for a zonal wavenumber kmax = 13'; with finite deformation radius 'the most unstable modes become kmax ~ 5-6'; lab 'jet equilibrates into a wavenumber-6 mode'. So wavenumber is set by jet instability scale relative to deformation radius. No Rossby-number rule confirmed (full paper not reached).

authors: Morales-Juberías, R.; Sayanagi, K. M.; Simon, A. A.; Fletcher, L. N.; Cosentino, R. G.
title: Meandering shallow atmospheric jet as a model of Saturn's north-polar hexagon
notes: Confirmed on IOP page (published 10 June 2015). Review arXiv:1609.09626: in the earlier Morales-Juberias et al. 2011 study the dominant wavenumber 'depends on the width of the initial jet', tuning it 'between 3 and 8'; in 2015 the vertical wind structure selects vortex street vs star-shaped vs polygonal meander; 'Saturn's 75N jet must be a shallow atmospheric structure'.
quantitative: Hexagon at ~78N, persisted >30 yr. Jet peak ~100 m/s. Model: deformation radius ~1100 km, bottom N = 6e-3 s^-1. Gaussian jet amplitude U0 and curvature b 'determine the dominant wavenumber' (both tuned to give n=6). Deep jets -> vortex streets (drift ~25 m/s); shallow jets -> meanders (drift ~3.1 m/s); bottom-decaying jet U0=125 m/s, b=10e-11 m^-1 s^-1 -> drift ~-0.3 m/s, matching hexagon (observed vertex speed 0.8+-1.1 m/s Voyager, -0.036+-0.004 m/s Cassini). Jets centred 40-75 deg did not go unstable in their tests per fetch summary; at 30-35 deg the result was Ribbon-like. Rossby number not used.

authors: O'Neill, M. E.; Emanuel, K. A.; Flierl, G. R.
title: Polar vortex formation in giant-planet atmospheres due to moist convection
notes: Confirmed on nature.com (online 15 June 2015, issue 7). A correction (sign in energy-parameter equation) was published, conclusions unaffected. Author preprint: https://core.ac.uk/download/78064588.pdf
quantitative: Abstract: polar flow type depends on two parameters: ratio of small-eddy (storm) size to planetary radius, and atmospheric energy density from moist-convective latent heating. Preprint: storm Burger number Br^2 = L_D^2 / storm size^2; energy parameter Ep = energy density scaled by Br^2 ('function of 11 parameters', poorly constrained). Nondimensional beta = L_D^2/(2a^2), so a/L_D = (2 beta)^(-1/2). 'Small' planets: L_D at most 30x smaller than a (a/L_D <= 30) -> with larger Ep, a strong symmetric largely barotropic polar cyclone; medium Ep -> asymmetric time-varying polar cyclone (Neptune-like, 'low Ep and high beta'). 'Large' planets: a/L_D >= 40 (small beta) -> multiple vortices, no polar concentration as Ep increases; low Ep -> weak eddy-driven jets, no polar cyclone. Ordering a/L_D: Jupiter > Saturn > Neptune; no numerical planet values given. Saturn = small-planet strong cyclone; Jupiter speculated to lack a single polar cyclone.

authors: Brueshaber, S. R.; Sayanagi, K. M.; Dowling, T. E.
title: Dynamical regimes of giant planet polar vortices
pages: 46-61 (start page 46 confirmed; end page not confirmed)
notes: DOI resolves to Elsevier pii S0019103518304810 (page not renderable). Citation 'Brueshaber, Sayanagi & Dowling 2019, Icarus 323, 46, doi:10.1016/j.icarus.2019.02.001' confirmed from reference list of arXiv:2206.08475. End page not confirmed: cite as 323, 46. Abstract itself not fetched.
quantitative: Secondary (arXiv:2006.14817, arXiv:2206.08475, Brueshaber 2020 WMU dissertation): Burger number Bu = (L_d/a)^2 (L_d deformation radius, a planetary radius); Bu was 'the most important dimensionless parameter'; 'As the Burger number is decreased a transition from Saturn-like to Jupiter-like polar cyclones is observed'. Small Bu -> multiple circumpolar cyclones (Jupiter); large Bu -> single pole-centred cyclone (Saturn, ice giants). Storm energetics did not play an important role in the equilibrated state. Numerical regime values from follow-up Brueshaber & Sayanagi 2021 (as quoted in arXiv:2206.08475): Saturn regime Bu ~1.6e-3, ice-giant regime Bu ~1e-2; Jupiter regime Bu ~1e-5 is arXiv:2206.08475 authors' framing. No explicit threshold numbers from the 2019 paper confirmed.

title: Waves and turbulence on a beta-plane
quantitative: Abstract writes the arrest wavenumber as k_beta = (beta/2U)^(1/2), U = r.m.s. particle speed. So the published length scale is 1/k_beta = (2U/beta)^(1/2); the common forms L = pi*sqrt(U/beta) or sqrt(U/beta) are later conventions, not the 1975 abstract's. Cascade rate T ~0.03 for 2D turbulence, falling ~5x at the wave transition; scales ~70 km (ocean), ~1000 km (atmosphere); cascade generates alternating zonal jets.

authors: Held, I. M.; Hou, A. Y.
title: Nonlinear axially symmetric circulations in a nearly inviscid atmosphere
notes: Confirmed on Princeton research portal (issue 3) and arXiv:2004.08414 reference list. AMS page rate-limited.
quantitative: Thermal Rossby number R = g H Delta_h / (Omega a)^2, with Delta_h the FRACTIONAL equator-pole radiative-equilibrium contrast (theta0*Delta_h = absolute) [arXiv:2004.08414]. Exact edge (x_H = sin phi_H) solves R = (3/4)[1/3 + 1/x^2 + x^2/(1-x^2) - (1/(2x^3)) ln((1+x)/(1-x))] [arXiv:2004.08414 eq. 32]. Small-angle/weak forcing: phi_H ~= (5R/3)^(1/2) [NOAA AOML lecture notes]. So phi_H ~= (5/3 * g H Delta_theta_h / (Omega^2 a^2 theta0))^(1/2) with Delta_theta_h absolute is the correct form. Not read from the original paper itself.
